## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.70838.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.70838.sa1)

In the interests of transparency, eLife publishes the most substantive revision requests and the accompanying author responses.

Acceptance summary:

During natural behavior, like chasing prey, animals make continuous body, eye and head movements. These change the specific retinotopic regions that process the target stimulus. Holmgren et al., describe a technical tour de force that allows for reconstruction of what mice exactly see during natural behavior. They find that during prey hunting, the mice's movements are coordinated in such a way that mice keep the prey in a specialized retinotopic region. This region has characteristic properties that appear optimized for visual processing of the prey.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Freely-moving mice visually pursue prey using a retinal area with least optic flow" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 2 peer reviewers, including Martin Vinck as Reviewing Editor and Reviewer #1, and the evaluation has been overseen by Tirin Moore as the Senior Editor.

The two reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission. Overall the reviewers were positive and appreciate the major technical tour de force to precisely monitor head and eye movements. The reviewers accept the statistical analyses and results. However they have concerns wrt the interpretation and to what extent the results are a consequence of the mouse simply running towards the cricket, or whether there is indeed something special about the specific binocular zone in which the cricket "lands". Addressing this should be a matter of enhancing the discussion, or if the authors want to make a strong claim adding some causal experiments.

Essential revisions:

1) A major concern is that readers will come away with the idea that the mouse is "foveating" the cricket and that there is something special about this location for optic flow, when both of these are consequences of the fact that the mouse is running toward the cricket. The authors should clarify what is active gaze control vs what is just a consequence of cricket pursuit. We encourage the authors that if they want to make a strong claim that this region is being actively used, there should be some causal support.

2) It would be useful to quantify whether the eye movements are strictly compensatory for head movements, or whether there are larger abrupts shift in gaze, as found in Michaiel.

3) Figures can be improved by labelling subpanels, as it is unclear what eg many of the circular plots represent without reading the caption.

4) The title is a bit misleading – it implies that mice are making active effort to use this region. Likewise, the abstract should note that both the specific retinal area and the optic flow pattern are direct consequences of running toward the cricket. And overall there is a lot of language that implies active targeting – the "the image of the prey is kept on a specific area". Since this is a consequence of the pursuit, rather than active maintaining the gaze, we suggest language more like "the image lands on a specific area" or "the image remains in a specific area".

5) If the authors want to support the inherent claim that this region is important for visually guided pursuit, which would provide more a significant advance, then some type of causal test would be helpful. Most conclusive would be a precise manipulation such as Johnson et al., 2020, e.g. manipulating α ganglion cells, or alternatively a lesion of the functional focus or blinders to occlude the functional focus.

6) The fact that the cricket does not land on the region of highest overall RGC density is a bit of an implausible strawman. Given that the cricket is in front of the mouse and that this region is located laterally (further than the amplitude of mouse eye movements) it's fairly clear that these will not overlap.

7) Johnson et al., (2021) provided a causal test demonstrating that mice not only use the binocular zone to pursue prey, but that the ipsi projecting RGCs that generate binocular receptive fields are necessary. This provides causal support for the findings demonstrated correlatively in this paper, yet this finding is not discussed beyond a reference to the fact that Johnson et al., also tracked head position during prey capture.

8) The authors emphasize that their setup eliminates auditory and olfactory cues. Is this essential to their results, i.e. do they find different targeting when these are not eliminated. Likewise, the title emphasizes visual pursuit, but does the cricket land on the same region when performing auditory pursuit (when controlled for pursuit accuracy?)

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

Holmgren et al., investigate how the head and eye movements in mice are coordinated during prey capture of crickets. A technical tour-de-force with eye and head tracking in freely moving animals allows for precise quantification of a cricket's position in the retinal field of view. Mice oriented towards the cricket using head rotations, maintaining the cricket in a narrow functional focus in the binocular, upper-temporal part of the retina. Eye movement were, as found in previous studies, primarily compensatory for head movements. The functional focus region has minimal optical flow and a high density region of α-ON retinal ganglion cells.

This is an impressive study, establishing a rich set of techniques for reconstruction of what the mice see during freely moving behavior, an approach that can be used for many different questions in the future. While some of the findings of the study are extensions of previous work, in particular, the compensatory head movements, the finding that during approach of the cricket it is kept within a relatively narrow functional focus with specialized properties is highly interesting. The finding will appeal to vision researchers, as well as researchers interested in the way in which our body optimizes sensory sampling of our environment according to ecological demands. The paper is well written and accessible to a broad audience.

An interesting question for future work would be to assess whether the head movements of the mice predict future trajectories of the cricket, thereby bringing the cricket into the predicted field of view, or whether the head movements are merely reactive to the cricket's behavior.

It would be useful to quantify whether the eye movements are strictly compensatory for head movements, or whether there are larger abrupts shift in gaze, as found in Michaiel.

A causal demonstration that silencing SC or V1 activity in this field of view disrupts behavior seems feasible and would provide direct support for the functional interpretations of the authors, but is not necessary for acceptance of the paper.

Figures can be improved by labelling subpanels, as it is unclear what eg many of the circular plots represent without reading the caption.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

This study aims to determine whether mice use a specific region of their visual field, and consequently retina, to pursues a target during natural behavior, prey capture. This is an interesting question because mice do not have a clear fovea like primates, and it is significant in the field since the mouse Is a common model system for vision. Recent studies have shown that eye movements in the mouse are mostly compensatory with saccades serving to reset eye centering, and that eye movements and direction of gaze are primarily driven by head movements (Meyer et al., 2020), including in prey capture (Michael et al., 2020). Likewise, mice accurately aim towards prey during pursuit (Hoy et al., 2016), and thus the prey is in the binocular zone based on amplitude of eye movements (Michael et al., 2020). Furthermore, a recent study (Johnson et al., 2021) used ablation of ipsi-projecting retinal ganglion cells to show that the binocular visual field is necessary for prey capture.

The authors use a tour-de-force computational approach to determine the visual scene as projected on to the retina, based on 3-D scanning and virtual reconstruction of the environment, improved eye tracking methods, and computational projection of the scene onto the retina, all while mice pursue and capture crickets. This novel and rigorous approach, which will likely be useful to others in the field, is a significant advance and the real strength of the paper. However, as discussed below, most of the results they obtain from this effort do not provide a clear advance beyond what was known from previous studies, and are largely a direct consequence of mice running towards crickets during pursuit, though the impression one gets from the title and abstract is that this is an active and optimal gaze targeting strategy. One significant new piece of knowledge is that the cricket image lands on the region of highest density of α retinal ganglion cells, and this might be something to emphasize or explore more fully.

1. A main finding is that the cricket is generally maintained in a specific location in the lower binocular zone, which they term a "functional focus". Furthermore, the authors do several tests as to whether this is an active centering process and conclude that is not. "Mice do not make compensatory vertical head movements, tracking eye movements or vergence eye movements to keep prey within their functional foci but instead retain their target within a restricted bearing by running straight towards it". Thus, this main finding is just a direct consequence of the fact that mice are pursuing crickets by running towards them. And indeed two previous papers (Michael et al., 2020, Johnson et al., 2021) showed that mice keep prey in their binocular zone and maintain their head tilted downward, so this is not necessarily new information.

2. The authors also ask "what advantage is this behavior to the mouse?" The obvious answer is that running straight toward crickets is how to catch them. In other words, this is not a gaze targeting strategy but simply a consequence of that fact that if you want to catch something, you run towards it. However, instead the authors analyze the pattern of optic flow and demonstrate that this places the cricket in the region of least optic flow. Again, this is likely a trivial consequence of the fact that mice are running straight towards the cricket. Translational motion results in a focus of expansion (FOE) of optic flow in the heading direction, and the FOE itself is a minimum in the optic flow. Hence, as long as the mice are running toward the cricket, it will be in a region that is on average (given distortions of optic flow resulting from eye movements) a minimum of optic flow. Therefore I don't see this as a significant finding, and particularly as the title, unless they can demonstrate that this is not trivially true.

3. The title is a bit misleading – it implies that mice are making active effort to use this region. Likewise, the abstract should note that both the specific retinal area and the optic flow pattern are direct consequences of running toward the cricket. And overall there is a lot of language that implies active targeting – the "the image of the prey is kept on a specific area". Since this is a consequence of the pursuit, rather than active maintaining the gaze, I'd suggest language more like "the image lands on a specific area" or "the image remains in a specific area".

4. If the authors want to support the inherent claim that this region is important for visually guided pursuit, which would provide more a significant advance, then some type of causal test would be helpful. Most conclusive would be a precise manipulation such as Johnson et al., 2020, e.g. manipulating α ganglion cells, or alternatively a lesion of the functional focus or blinders to occlude the functional focus.

5. The fact that the cricket does not land on the region of highest overall RGC density is a bit of an implausible strawman. Given that the cricket is in front of the mouse and that this region is located laterally (further than the amplitude of mouse eye movements) it's fairly clear that these will not overlap.

6. Johnson et al., (2021) provided a causal test demonstrating that mice not only use the binocular zone to pursue prey, but that the ipsi projecting RGCs that generate binocular receptive fields are necessary. This provides causal support for the findings demonstrated correlatively in this paper, yet this finding is not discussed beyond a reference to the fact that Johnson et al., also tracked head position during prey capture.

7. The authors emphasize that their setup eliminates auditory and olfactory cues. Is this essential to their results, i.e. do they find different targeting when these are not eliminated. Likewise, the title emphasizes visual pursuit, but does the cricket land on the same region when performing auditory pursuit (when controlled for pursuit accuracy?)

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Visual pursuit behavior in mice maintains the pursued prey on the retinal region with least optic flow" for further consideration by eLife. Your revised article has been evaluated by Tirin Moore (Senior Editor) and a Reviewing Editor.

The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed before final acceptance, as outlined below. These can be addressed with textual changes. Please clearly indicate those changes so we can proceed with acceptance as soon as possible.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

The authors have addressed all of my comments.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

The authors have overall done an excellent job of revising their claims to match the data and avoid misleading conclusions by readers. I have two remaining points that weren't fully addressed.

1. The authors have generally improved the wording in the text to avoid implying that mice are actively targeting the cricket to this region. However, this is still not very clearly stated in the abstract, which is what most people take away from a paper. Indeed, in their response, the authors state that their findings are best stated in the first paragraph of the discussion as "The positional maintenance of the cricket was not achieved by active eye movements that followed the prey, but rather by the animal's change in behavior, specifically the head-movement and orientation towards the prey during pursuit." A statement along these lines in the abstract would be very effective, so that readers don't have to wait until the discussion to have this stated explicitly. If word length is the issue, I suggest finding something else to trim since as the authors themselves note, this is the best statement of the conclusion from their findings.

2. In the public section of the original review, I noted that the fact that the cricket lands in the region of least motion blur was an almost trivial consequence of the fact that the mouse is running towards the cricket, and hence the cricket is at the focus of expansion (minimum of optic flow). However, this has not been addressed in the revision – I apologize if that is because it was in the public comments rather than author comments. However, it seems essential to address this so that readers do not think that this is an "design principle" of mouse vision. Unless the authors can provide a compelling argument for how this could not be the case, given the geometry of optic flow, then the statement that it lands on the region of least motion blur should be accompanied, in the abstract and elsewhere, by the clarification that this is a direct consequence of motion towards the cricket rather than a specific optimality. I also suggest revising the title to emphasize a more compelling finding (e.g. α RGCs), but if the authors want to continue to use this title, accompanied by appropriate explanation in the abstract, then that is their prerogative.

claims.claim: Mouse retina contains retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) with a broad diversity of functional classes.
claims.source: Mouse retina contains retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), the output cells of the retina, with a broad diversity of functional classes (Baden et al., 2016; Bleckert et al., 2014; Franke et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Cited from multiple studies characterizing RGC diversity.

claims.claim: The highest overall density of RGCs faces laterally given the lateral eye position.
claims.source: Given the lateral eye position, the highest overall density faces laterally (Dräger and Olsen, 1981; Sabbah et al., 2017; Salinas-Navarro et al., 2009; Stabio et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Cited from multiple anatomical studies of mouse retina.

claims.claim: Functionally defined ganglion cells and cone sub-types are segregated into retinal subregions within the large stabilized field of view.
claims.source: Further, as the functionally defined ganglion cells (Baden et al., 2016; Bleckert et al., 2014; Franke et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2012) and cone sub-types (Szél et al., 1992) are segregated into retinal subregions within the large stabilized field of view, recent studies suggest that retinal subregions are tuned for specific behavioral tasks depending on what part of the world they subtend (Baden et al., 2016; Bleckert et al., 2014; Hughes, 1977; Sabbah et al., 2017; Szatko et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Cited from multiple studies on retinal organization and function.

claims.claim: Upon cricket detection, mice oriented and ran towards the cricket, resulting in a significant adjustment to their trajectory.
claims.source: Upon cricket detection, mice oriented and ran towards the cricket, resulting in a significant adjustment to their trajectory (Δ target bearing: 40.2 ± 35.1°, P = 6.20 x 10−10, Δ speed: 10.2 ± 7.4 cm/s, P = 1.91 x 10−10; N=57 detect-track sequences N = 3 mice; Paired Wilcoxon's signed rank test for both tests)
claims.evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data with specific values and significance tests.

claims.claim: During tracking, the cricket was kept in front of the mouse, resulting in a significant reduction in the spread of target bearings compared to during detect epochs.
claims.source: During tracking, the cricket was kept in front of the mouse, resulting in a significant reduction in the spread of target bearings compared to during detect epochs (Figure 2D, Target bearing: detect 6.2 ± 62.1°, track: 2.5 ± 25.6°, mean ± SD, Brown-Forsythe test p = 0, F statistic=7.05x103, N=4406 detect and 13624 track frames, N=3 mice), consistent with previous findings (Hoy et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison of behavioral data with reference to previous study.

claims.claim: The location of the cricket image during the tracking phase was significantly different from the cluster in the detect epoch.
claims.source: average histogram of the location of cricket image during tracking phase vs average histogram of the location of cricket during detect phase: Left eye P = 3.54 x 10−46, Right eye P = 1.08 x 10−81, differences calculated by taking the Mean Absolute Difference with bootstrapping, N=57 detect-track sequences, N = 3 mice
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison of cricket position distributions between behavioral epochs.

claims.claim: The functional focus fell within the binocular field.
claims.source: Thus, during the tracking and pursuit behavior the image of the prey consistently fell on a local and specific retinal area that we refer to from here on as the functional focus. The functional focus fell within the binocular field
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 2G-H with functional focus located in binocular region.

claims.claim: The region of elevated density of RGCs has been found to be located near the optical axis.
claims.source: while the region of elevated density of RGCs has been found to be located near the optical axis (Dräger and Olsen, 1981)
claims.evidence: Cited from anatomical study of mouse retina.

claims.claim: The location of the retinal specialization may not overlap with the functional focus.
claims.source: which suggests that the location of the retinal specialization may not overlap with the functional focus.
claims.evidence: Inferred from comparison of RGC density location and functional focus location.

claims.claim: The gain of compensation for head pitch and roll rotations was relatively linear and less than unity, indicating on average under-compensation of the head rotation.
claims.source: The gain of this compensation was relatively linear and less than unity for both pitch- and roll-axes, indicating on average under-compensation of the head rotation (slope (gain) of relation for pitch axis, −0.45 ± 0.12 and −0.48 ± 0.06; roll axis −0.51 ± 0.12 and −0.62 ± 0.05 for left and right eye respectively, 168852 frames, N=3 mice).
claims.evidence: Quantitative analysis of head-eye rotation relationships from experimental data.

claims.claim: For rotations around the head x-axis (head pitch changes) the gain of compensation was most affected by freezing torsional rotations.
claims.source: For rotations around the head x-axis (head pitch changes) the gain of compensation was most affected by freezing torsional rotations (Figure 4C, gain mean ± SD, control: −0.45 ± 0.12and-0.48 ± 0.06; torsion frozen −0.24 ± 0.1 and −0.24 ± 0.01, for left and right eyes respectively, N = 168852 frames, N=3 mice)
claims.evidence: Computational analysis freezing specific eye rotation axes to assess their contribution.

claims.claim: The gain of compensation for rotations around the head y-axis (head roll changes) was dramatically affected by freezing vertical rotations.
claims.source: The gain of compensation for rotations around the head y-axis (head roll changes) was dramatically affected by freezing vertical rotations (Figure 4C, gain mean ± SD, control: −0.51 ± 0.12 and −0.62 ± 0.05, vertical frozen −0.16 ± 0.14 and −0.17 ± 0.03, for left and right eyes respectively, N = 168852 frames, N=3 mice)
claims.evidence: Computational analysis freezing specific eye rotation axes to assess their contribution.

claims.claim: The functional foci for both eyes were predominately contained within the region of continuous binocular overlap.
claims.source: The functional foci for both eyes were predominately contained within the region of continuous binocular overlap.
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 4D with functional foci overlaid on binocular overlap probability map.

claims.claim: The mean alignment of the reference point over all animals and data segments was approximately 8-9 degrees.
claims.source: the mean alignment of the reference point over all animals and data segments being ~8–9°, which is around the size of V1 cortical neuron receptive fields (~5–15° [Niell and Stryker, 2008], Figure 4H, mean ± SD, left eye projected into right eye 8.8 ± 6.9°; right eye projected into left eye 8.6 ± 6.7°).
claims.evidence: Quantitative analysis of inter-ocular alignment with comparison to V1 receptive field sizes.

claims.claim: Freezing the movements of one eye to its mean position resulted in a significant increase in the alignment error.
claims.source: Coordination of eye movements was important for alignment, as freezing the movements of one eye to its mean position resulted in a significant increase in the alignment error when comparing individual cricket tracking sequences (left all rotations vs. left eye frozen P = 1.78 x 10−10, right eye all rotations vs. right eye frozen P = 7.12 x 10−11, N=52 sequences, unpaired Student's t-test)
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison of alignment with and without eye movements frozen.

claims.claim: As the mouse approached the cricket during the track behavioral epoch, the projected cricket positions systematically shifted lower in the visual field.
claims.source: As the mouse approached the cricket during the track behavioral epoch, the projected cricket positions systematically shifted lower in the visual field (Figure 5A lower).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 5A with cricket positions color-coded by distance.

claims.claim: Mice did not use additional head or eye movements to bring the cricket into the functional foci.
claims.source: This suggests that the mice did not use additional head or eye movements (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) to bring the cricket into the functional foci, but rather manipulated the cricket's position in the eye view by orienting and moving towards the target.
claims.evidence: Inferred from systematic shift in cricket position and lack of compensatory head/eye movements.

claims.claim: Head pitch remained stable as the mice approached the crickets.
claims.source: Consistent with this, head pitch remained stable as the mice approached the crickets (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 5B plotting head pitch vs distance to cricket.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference in head pitch as a function of distance to the cricket between non-tracking and tracking periods.
claims.source: Furthermore, there was no significant difference in head pitch as a function of distance to the cricket between non-tracking and tracking periods (non-tracking head pitch: −3.7 ± 26.5°, mean ± SD, median = −11.3°, tracking head pitch: −12.9 ± 15.7°, mean ± SD, median = −14.6°, Ks test, P = 0.709, paired Student's t-test P = 0.197, N = 18 non-tracking and track sequences, N = 3 mice).
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison of head pitch between behavioral epochs.

claims.claim: Mice did not significantly converge their eyes as they approached the crickets.
claims.source: In addition, and consistent with previous findings (Michaiel et al., 2020), mice did not significantly converge their eyes as they approached the crickets (non-tracking head vergence: 7.6 ± 13.5°, mean ± SD, median = 8.6°, tracking head vergence: 2.5 ± 16.7°, mean ± SD, median = 3.2°. Ks test, P = 0.425, paired Student's t-test P = 0.225, N=18 non-tracking and track sequences, N = 3 mice, Figure 5—figure supplement 1J and Table 4).
claims.evidence: Statistical analysis of vergence with citation to previous study.

claims.claim: During cricket tracking periods, mice ran directly toward the cricket, and their trajectories were significantly straighter than during equivalent non-tracking phases.
claims.source: During cricket tracking periods, mice ran directly toward the cricket, and their trajectories were significantly straighter than during equivalent non-tracking phases (Figure 5C–G).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 5C-G with multiple trajectory metrics compared between epochs.

claims.claim: Lateral deviation at the half-way point was significantly smaller in the tracking epochs compared to non-tracking epochs.
claims.source: Lateral deviation at the half-way point (Figure 5E, non-tracking 4.3 ± 4.0 cm, tracking 1.4 ± 2.0 cm, p = 0.009)
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison of trajectory metrics between behavioral epochs.

claims.claim: Maximum lateral deviation was significantly smaller in tracking epochs compared to non-tracking epochs.
claims.source: maximum lateral deviation (Figure 5F, non-tracking, 7.7 ± 4.9 cm, tracking 2.8 ± 2.0 cm, p = 0.0006)
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison of trajectory metrics between behavioral epochs.

claims.claim: The area between the trajectory and minimum distance path to the target was significantly smaller in tracking epochs compared to non-tracking epochs.
claims.source: the area between the trajectory and minimum distance path to the target (Figure 5G, area under the curve, non-tracking 135.6 ± 102.7 cm2, tracking 51.3 ± 45.8 cm2, p = 0.0029)
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison of trajectory metrics between behavioral epochs.

claims.claim: Mice do not make compensatory vertical head movements, tracking eye movements or vergence eye movements to keep prey within their functional foci.
claims.source: Together this suggests that mice do not make compensatory vertical head movements, tracking eye movements or vergence eye movements to keep prey within their functional foci, but instead retain their target within a restricted bearing by running straight towards it.
claims.evidence: Inferred from analysis of head and eye movements during pursuit.

claims.claim: Optic flow is minimized in the direction of travel directly in front of the animal.
claims.source: Optic flow is minimized in the direction of travel directly in front of the animal (Sabbah et al., 2017), with flow fields directed away from the travel direction and forming a second minimum directly behind the animal's head (Figure 6A, see also Angelaki and Hess, 2005).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous studies on optic flow.

claims.claim: Mice have laterally facing eyes with optical axis approximately 60 degrees lateral of frontal.
claims.source: As mice have laterally facing eyes (optical axis = 59.9 ± 19.8° and −62.3 ± 14.7° lateral of frontal for the left and right eyes respectively, N=3 mice)
claims.evidence: Measured from anatomical calibration data.

claims.claim: Idealized forward motion resulted in the region of minimal optic flow in each eye being located off optical axis in the ventro-medial corneal region representing the animal's forward direction.
claims.source: idealized forward motion resulted in the region of minimal optic flow in each eye being located off optical axis in the ventro-medial corneal region representing the animal's forward direction (radial displacement from optical axis 36.64 ± 0.92° and −41.11 ± 2.27°, rotational angle 122.95 ± 17.05° and −107.94 ± 9.96°, for the left and right eyes respectively, mean ± SD, N=2 mice, Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: Calculated from idealized optic flow simulation.

claims.claim: Optic flow in the 30x30° region surrounding the ventro-medial point of minimal optic flow was significantly lower than that in an equivalent region in the ventro-temporal region during free movement.
claims.source: Optic flow in the 30x30° region surrounding the ventro-medial point of minimal optic flow was significantly lower than that in an equivalent region in the ventro-temporal region during free movement, but not in the simulated case (free movement: nasal 46.3 ± 9.8 °/s, temporal: 199.4 ± 29.0 °/s, p = 0.0014, simulated: nasal 163.6 ± 82.2 °/s, temporal: 833.0 ± 416.5 °/s, p = 0.0662, mean ± SD, two-sided t-test, unequal variance, N=2 mice).
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison of optic flow in different regions.

claims.claim: Optic flow was higher in the lower visual field and considerably lower in the upper visual field.
claims.source: Optic flow was higher in the lower visual field and considerably lower in the upper visual field (lower left eye visual field: 262.44 ± 106.50 °/s, upper left eye visual field: 44.87 ± 24.31 °/s, p = 1.78x10−20, lower right eye visual field: 361.91 ± 168.80 °/s, upper right eye visual field: 40.59 ± 22.79 °/s, p = 6.68x10−19, Two-sided t-test, unequal variance, N=2 mice)
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison of optic flow in upper vs lower visual fields.

claims.claim: The region of highest likelihood for the presence of the optic flow minimum overlapped considerably with the functional foci in both eyes during the tracking epochs of the pursuit behavior.
claims.source: The region of highest likelihood for the presence of the optic flow minimum overlapped considerably with the functional foci in both eyes during the tracking epochs of the pursuit behavior (overlap of optic flow 95% minima and functional foci 50% regions: 100% and 99 ± 1%, overlap of optic flow 50% minima and functional foci 50% regions: 61 ± 14% and 72 ± 4% in left and right eyes respectively, N=3 mice, Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: Quantitative overlap analysis between optic flow minima and functional foci.

claims.claim: The behavioral strategy employed by mice during hunting results in the image of their prey coinciding with the region of reduced optic flow during pursuit.
claims.source: Together this shows that the behavioral strategy employed by mice during hunting, consisting of orienting themselves to directly face the prey and following a straight and direct course to it, results in the image of their prey coinciding with the region of reduced optic flow during pursuit, where the retinal image of their prey is least distorted due to motion induced image blur.
claims.evidence: Synthesized conclusion from optic flow and behavioral trajectory analyses.

claims.claim: Eye rotations in mice primarily stabilize their large field of view and all three rotational axes, including ocular torsion, combine to counter head rotations.
claims.source: This strongly suggested that eye-rotations in mice, like in rats, primarily stabilize their large field of view and that all three rotational axes, including ocular torsion, combine to counter head rotations.
claims.evidence: Inferred from analysis of head-eye rotation relationships across all three axes.

claims.claim: Eye rotations cannot be predicted from head rotations in any one axis but rather by a combination of all head rotations.
claims.source: In addition, we also show that eye rotations cannot be predicted from head rotations in any one axis as has been suggested by recent studies of mouse eye motion (Meyer et al., 2020; Meyer et al., 2018; Michaiel et al., 2020) but rather by a combination of all head rotations (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 with model predictions using single vs multiple head rotation axes.

claims.claim: The location of the functional focus occurs within a dorso-temporal retinal region in an area with the highest density of Alpha-ON sustained RGCs.
claims.source: Using this we show that the location of the functional focus occurs within a dorso-temporal retinal region in an area with the highest density of Alpha-ON sustained RGCs, whose general properties have been previously proposed to be well suited for this purpose (Bleckert et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Shown through eye model projection and overlap analysis with RGC density maps.

claims.claim: The binocular region of the visual field in mice is contained within the nasal visual field of each eye, and spans a region of 30-40° in front of the animal.
claims.source: Both estimates of the field of view of the mouse eye (Dräger, 1978) and electrophysiological measurements of receptive field locations of visually responsive neurons (Dräger and Olsen, 1980; Wagor et al., 1980) have established that the binocular region of the visual field in mice is contained within the nasal visual field of each eye, and spans a region of 30-40° in front of the animal (Wagor et al., 1980).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous anatomical and electrophysiological studies.

claims.claim: The overlapping monocular fields that make up the binocular overlap are not constantly maintained but fluctuate at the margins as the eyes rotate to counter head rotations.
claims.source: We present here, that similar to the rat (Wallace et al., 2013), the overlapping monocular fields that make up the binocular overlap are not constantly maintained (Figure 4H) but fluctuate at the margins as the eyes rotate to counter head rotations (Figure 4D), resulting in a region where there is a transition from one area with near continuous binocular coverage, through to a region that is invariably monocular.
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 4D and 4H with binocular overlap probability maps.

claims.claim: The functional focus lies within the region of high probability of maintained binocular overlap.
claims.source: The functional focus described here lies within the region of high probability of maintained binocular overlap.
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 4D with functional focus overlaid on binocular overlap map.

claims.claim: The temporal retina contains both ipsilaterally projecting (uncrossed) RGCs and RGCs which form part of the callosal projection pathway.
claims.source: This region of the visual field projects onto the temporal retina, which contains both ipsilaterally projecting (uncrossed) RGCs (Dräger and Olsen, 1980; Reese and Cowey, 1986) and RGCs which form part of the callosal projection pathway (Laing et al., 2015; Olavarria and Van Sluyters, 1983; Ramachandra et al., 2020), both of which are considered central to binocular visual processing.
claims.evidence: Cited from multiple studies on retinal projections.

claims.claim: The functional focus location is well placed to support stereoscopic depth perception.
claims.source: In addition, the current study adds to the significance of these previous findings and suggests that the functional focus location is well placed to support stereoscopic depth perception, assuming that this form of visual processing is available to and employed by the mouse (La Chioma et al., 2019; La Chioma et al., 2020; Samonds et al., 2019; Scholl et al., 2013; Scholl et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Inferred from functional focus location in binocular region with citations to studies on mouse stereopsis.

claims.claim: Selective ablation of ipsilaterally projecting RGCs in the ventro-temporal retina reduced the probability that coming into close proximity with the cricket resulted in its capture.
claims.source: Further supportive of the importance and relevance of the region of binocular overlap, another recent study provides strong evidence to suggest that ipsilaterally projecting RGCs in the ventro-temporal retina are important in the final phase of cricket pursuit (mouse to cricket distance less than 6 cm), with selective ablation of these RGCs reducing the probability that coming into close proximity with the cricket resulted in its capture (Johnson et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Cited from recent study on RGC function in prey capture.

claims.claim: The overall highest density of retinal ganglion cells in mice is located in the region around the optical axis.
claims.source: While the overall highest density of retinal ganglion cells in mice is located in the region around the optical axis (Dräger and Olsen, 1981)
claims.evidence: Cited from anatomical study of mouse retina.

claims.claim: The highest density of Alpha-ON sustained RGCs resides in the superior-temporal retina.
claims.source: a recent study examining the distributions of various different subclasses of RGCs has shown that the highest density of Alpha-ON sustained RGCs resides in the superior-temporal retina (Bleckert et al., 2014)
claims.evidence: Cited from study on RGC subtype distributions.

claims.claim: Alpha-ON sustained RGCs have center-surround receptive fields, a rapid response and fast conducting axon, and are thought to be 'spot detectors'.
claims.source: These Alpha-ON sustained RGCs have center-surround receptive fields, a rapid response and fast conducting axon, and are thought to be 'spot detectors' (for review see Dhande et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Cited from review on RGC properties.

claims.claim: Alpha-ON sustained RGCs in the superior-temporal retinal region have a significantly smaller dendritic tree radius and subtend a smaller area of physical space as well as have overlapping receptive fields compared to the same RGC-type in other regions of the retina.
claims.source: In addition, the Alpha-ON sustained RGCs in this particular retinal region differ from the same RGC-type in other regions of the retina as they have a significantly smaller dendritic tree radius and subtend a smaller area of physical space as well as have overlapping receptive fields (Bleckert et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Cited from study on regional RGC properties.

claims.claim: The cellular properties of Alpha-ON sustained RGCs as well as the region in-front of the animal which provides their input are consistent with the requirements for tracking small and mobile targets.
claims.source: Taken together, the cellular properties as well as the region in-front of the animal which provides their input are consistent with the requirements for tracking small and mobile targets (Bleckert et al., 2014; Dean et al., 1989; Lettvin et al., 1959; Procacci et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Synthesized from RGC properties with citations to studies on target tracking.

claims.claim: Both wide-field and narrow-field neuronal types in the mouse superior colliculus play central roles in the detection and pursuit phases of prey pursuit, respectively.
claims.source: A recent study has shown that both wide-field and narrow-field neuronal types in the mouse superior colliculus play central roles in the detection and pursuit phases of this pursuit task, respectively (Hoy et al., 2019)
claims.evidence: Cited from study on superior colliculus function in prey pursuit.

claims.claim: Alpha-ON sustained RGCs have projections to the superior colliculus.
claims.source: and consistent with this, Alpha-ON sustained RGCs having projections to the superior colliculus (Martersteck et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Cited from study on RGC projection patterns.

claims.claim: Alpha RGCs have strong projections to the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus and thus V1.
claims.source: It is currently unclear how the primary visual cortex (V1) contributes to this behavior, but some role is possible if not probable, which would also be supported by the strong Alpha RGC projection to the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus and thus V1 (Martersteck et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Cited from study on RGC projection patterns with speculation about V1 role.

claims.claim: An increased cortical magnification factor occurs in the region corresponding to the nasal, binocular visual field.
claims.source: Additionally, an increased cortical magnification factor occurs in the region corresponding to the nasal, binocular visual field (Garrett et al., 2014; Schuett et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: Cited from studies on cortical visual field representation.

claims.claim: Global alignment across the retina of the preferred orientation of direction-selective retinal ganglion cells with the cardinal directions of optic flow during idealized motion has been shown in mice.
claims.source: Mechanistically supporting this, global alignment across the retina of the preferred orientation of direction-selective retinal ganglion cells with the cardinal directions of optic flow during idealized motion has been shown in mice (Sabbah et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Cited from study on direction-selective RGC organization.

claims.claim: Ocular torsion in freely moving rats is correlated with head pitch such that nose-up rotation of the head is counteracted by incyclotorsion of both eyes, with nose-down pitch counteracted by excyclotorsion.
claims.source: In freely moving rats, it has been shown that ocular torsion is correlated with head pitch such that nose-up rotation of the head is counteracted by incyclotorsion (rotation toward the nose) of both eyes, with nose-down pitch counteracted by excyclotorsion (Wallace et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Cited from previous study on rat VOR.

claims.claim: Torsional rotation in freely moving mice is dynamic, with episodes showing in- and excyclovergence as well as dextro- and levocycloversion.
claims.source: We show here that torsional rotation in freely moving mice is also dynamic, with episodes showing in- and excyclovergence as well as dextro- and levocycloversion.
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 with examples of different torsional coordination patterns.

claims.claim: There was an additional relation between ocular torsion and head roll consistent with VOR-evoked dextro- and levocycloversion.
claims.source: Further, while the correlation between torsional rotation and head pitch observed in rats was measured, there was also an additional relation between ocular torsion and head roll consistent with VOR-evoked dextro- and levocycloversion.
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2L-M with correlation between torsion and head roll.

claims.claim: Prediction of torsion using a model based on head pitch alone resulted in an average error of around 7°.
claims.source: Consequently, prediction of torsion using a model based on head pitch alone resulted in an average error of around 7°, while an expanded model including roll as well performed better (Figure 4—figure supplement 2J–O).
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2J-O comparing model predictions.

claims.claim: During pursuit in mice the image of the intended prey falls consistently in a localized region of their visual fields through the animal orientating their head and body and running directly toward the prey rather than with specific eye movements.
claims.source: In summary, we show here that during pursuit in mice the image of the intended prey falls consistently in a localized region of their visual fields, referred to here as the functional focus, and that this occurs through the animal orientating their head and body and running directly toward the prey rather than with specific eye movements.
claims.evidence: Summary conclusion synthesized from behavioral and eye movement analyses.

claims.claim: The location of the functional focus is within the binocular visual field and coincides with the region of minimal optic flow during the pursuit.
claims.source: The location of the functional focus is within the binocular visual field, but in addition also coincides with the region of minimal optic flow during the pursuit, and presumably also minimally distorted by motion blur.
claims.evidence: Summary conclusion from binocular overlap and optic flow analyses.

claims.claim: Experiments were carried out using male C57Bl/6J mice acquired from Charles River Laboratories.
claims.source: Experiments were carried out using male C57Bl/6J mice acquired from Charles River Laboratories.
claims.evidence: Stated in Materials and methods.

claims.claim: At the time of the cricket hunting experiments, mice were between 2 and 8 months old, and weighed between 21 and 29 g.
claims.source: At the time of the cricket hunting experiments, mice (n=9) were between 2 and 8 months old, and weighed between 21 and 29 g.
claims.evidence: Stated in Materials and methods.

claims.claim: During experiments in which head and eye rotations were recorded cricket body sizes ranged from 1 cm to 2 cm.
claims.source: During experiments in which head and eye rotations were recorded cricket body sizes ranged from 1 cm to 2 cm (1.8 ± 0.3 cm, mean ± SD, n=25).
claims.evidence: Stated in Materials and methods.

claims.claim: The average differences in position of fiducial points between the two coordinate systems were less than 1 mm.
claims.source: The average differences in position of fiducial points between the two coordinate systems were less than 1 mm (mean ± SD, x position, 0.18 ± 3.1 mm, y position, 0.07 ± 1.6 mm, z position, 0.66 ± 1.8 mm, N=54 fiducial points from three datasets).
claims.evidence: Stated in Results describing coordinate system registration accuracy.

claims.claim: The average 50% contour of the functional focus was overlapped by the highest density of Alpha-ON sustained RGC's by 35% and 67% for left and right eye respectively.
claims.source: The average 50% contour of the functional focus was overlapped by the highest density of Alpha-ON sustained RGC's by 35% and 67% for left and right eye respectively (Figure 3E, black, mean ± SD for left and right eye, 35.1 ± 19.8%, 66.7 ± 0.09%, p = 0.095 and 0.019, one-sided Student's t-test)
claims.evidence: Quantitative overlap analysis with statistical testing.

claims.claim: The overlap of the functional focus with the second highest density of Alpha-ON sustained RGCs was 83% and 95% for left and right eye respectively.
claims.source: and the overlap with the second highest density was 83% and 95% (mean ± SD for left and right eye, 82.8 ± 20.1%, 94.8 ± 24.7%, p = 0.042 and 0.003, one-sided Student's t-test)
claims.evidence: Quantitative overlap analysis with statistical testing.

claims.claim: There is a high degree of correspondence between the highest density of Alpha-ON sustained RGC's and the functional focus during pursuit behavior.
claims.source: suggesting a high degree of correspondence between the highest density of Alpha-ON sustained RGC's and the functional focus during pursuit behavior.
claims.evidence: Inferred from overlap analysis results.

claims.claim: Objects falling within the functional foci are processed by Alpha-ON sustained RGC's.
claims.source: Together this suggests that objects falling within the functional foci are processed by Alpha-ON sustained RGC's.
claims.evidence: Inferred from spatial correspondence between functional foci and Alpha-ON sustained RGC density.

claims.claim: Torsional rotations in freely moving mice spanned a wide range of rotation angles.
claims.source: As with the vertical and horizontal rotations (Meyer et al., 2018), torsional rotations in freely moving mice spanned a wide range of rotation angles (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D)
claims.evidence: Shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-D with distribution of torsional angles.

claims.claim: Torsional rotations were correlated with head pitch with Pearson's correlation coefficient of -0.72 and 0.58 for detect, and -0.60 and 0.53 for track in left and right eyes respectively.
claims.source: and were correlated with head pitch (Pearson's correlation coefficient (r): detect −0.72, 0.58, track: −0.60 and 0.53 for left and right eyes respectively, N=4406 detect and 13624 track frames, N=3 mice, Figure 4—figure supplement 2C–D)
claims.evidence: Correlation analysis of torsion and head pitch.

claims.claim: Torsional rotations were correlated with head roll with Pearson's correlation coefficient of -0.46 and -0.47 for detect, and -0.45 and -0.48 for track in left and right eyes respectively.
claims.source: as well as head roll (Pearson's correlation coefficient (r): detect: −0.46, –0.47 track: −0.45 and −0.48 for left and right eyes respectively, N=4406 detect and 13624 track frames, N=3 mice, Figure 4—figure supplement 2L–M)
claims.evidence: Correlation analysis of torsion and head roll.

claims.claim: The functional foci were directed at the region in front of the animal's nose and within the region of stable binocular overlap.

results.result: During prey pursuit, mice maintain the cricket image within a localized retinal region termed the 'functional focus' through behavioral orientation rather than active eye movements. This functional focus is located within the binocular visual field and is maintained by the mouse orienting toward and running directly at the prey.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C12-C15, and C64 provide converging evidence from behavioral tracking (C12-C13), statistical analysis of cricket position distributions (C14), and visual field mapping (C2, C15) that collectively demonstrate prey images consistently fall within a localized functional focus. The behavioral mechanism is well-characterized through trajectory analysis and the absence of compensatory eye movements.

results.result: The functional focus coincides with the region of minimal optic flow in the visual field during pursuit. This overlap occurs because mice run directly toward prey, placing the prey image in the ventro-medial region where optic flow is minimized, thereby reducing motion-induced image blur.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C39, and C40 demonstrate substantial overlap (61-100%) between functional foci and optic flow minima through quantitative analysis. Supporting claims C34-C38 establish the theoretical and empirical basis for optic flow patterns. The behavioral strategy (C40, C65) mechanistically links straight-line pursuit to reduced optic flow, with statistical support from multiple comparisons.

results.result: The functional focus is located in the dorso-temporal retina and overlaps with the high-density region of Alpha-ON sustained retinal ganglion cells (RGCs). These RGCs possess properties (center-surround receptive fields, rapid response, small dendritic trees with overlapping receptive fields) consistent with tracking small mobile targets.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C71 provide quantitative overlap data (35-95% depending on density threshold and eye) with statistical significance (p<0.05). The anatomical correspondence (C4, C43, C79) is supported by eye model projections. RGC properties (C52-C53) are cited from established literature (Bleckert et al., 2014; Dhande et al., 2015), and the functional interpretation (C54, C73) reasonably follows from the spatial and cellular evidence.

results.result: Eye rotations in all three axes (horizontal, vertical, torsional) combine to stabilize the visual field through the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR). Torsional rotations are critical for compensating head pitch, while vertical rotations are essential for compensating head roll. Eye rotations cannot be predicted from head rotations in a single axis but require consideration of all three head rotation axes.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C20 provide quantitative gain measurements with computational validation through axis-freezing experiments (N=168,852 frames, N=3 mice). Claims C74-C76 establish torsional rotation correlations with both pitch (r=-0.72 to 0.58) and roll (r=-0.45 to -0.48). Claim C42 demonstrates improved model performance when using multiple axes. The evidence converges to support the multi-axis VOR mechanism (C41, C80).

results.result: The functional foci are located within the region of stable binocular overlap, with inter-ocular alignment maintained at approximately 8-10 degrees through coordinated eye movements. Freezing eye movements significantly increases alignment error by ~54%, demonstrating the importance of VOR-mediated coordination for binocular alignment.
results.evaluation: Claims C21, C46, and C77 establish the functional focus location within binocular overlap through probability mapping. Claims C22 and C82 quantify alignment precision (~8-9°) comparable to V1 receptive field sizes. Claim C23 provides statistical evidence (p<10^-10) that eye movements are necessary for maintaining alignment, with C83 quantifying the 54% increase in error when movements are frozen. The binocular field properties (C44-C45) are supported by cited literature.

results.result: Mice maintain prey within the functional focus through direct pursuit behavior (running straight toward the target) rather than through compensatory head pitch adjustments, vergence eye movements, or tracking eye movements. During tracking, mice exhibit significantly straighter trajectories than during non-tracking periods.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C28 provide statistical evidence (p>0.19) showing no significant changes in head pitch or vergence as mice approach prey. Claims C29-C32 demonstrate significantly straighter trajectories during tracking (p<0.01 for multiple metrics). Claim C24 shows systematic downward shift of cricket position with approach, and C25 infers the absence of compensatory movements. The behavioral mechanism (C33) is well-supported by converging negative and positive evidence.

results.result: Removing both olfactory and auditory cues approximately doubled cricket capture time compared to removing auditory cues alone, demonstrating that vision is sufficient but less efficient for prey capture when other sensory modalities are masked.
results.evaluation: Claim C6 provides statistical evidence (p=0.0471, Wilcoxon rank sum test) with specific values (control: 24.92±16.77s vs. cues removed: 43.51±27.82s) from N=13 control and N=12 experimental trials across N=5 mice. The experimental design appropriately isolates visual guidance, supporting the study's focus on visual pursuit mechanisms.

results.result: The region of highest overall RGC density is located near the optical axis and directed laterally, which is spatially distinct from the functional focus location. This suggests that total RGC density does not predict functional specialization for prey pursuit.
results.evaluation: Claims C16 and C50 cite established anatomical literature (Dräger and Olsen, 1981) for RGC density location. Claim C78 provides quantitative directional data (azimuth: -66.2±6.7° and 70.3±4.7°) showing lateral orientation. Claim C17 appropriately infers the spatial mismatch between total RGC density and functional focus, which is further supported by the eye model projections in Figure 3.

results.result: The temporal retina containing the functional focus projects to brain regions involved in binocular processing (ipsilateral projections, callosal pathway) and prey pursuit (superior colliculus, dLGN/V1). This anatomical organization supports potential roles in stereoscopic depth perception and visually-guided hunting behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C47, C55-C58 are well-supported by multiple anatomical and functional studies cited in the text. Claim C49 cites recent evidence (Johnson et al., 2021) that ipsilateral RGC ablation impairs final capture phase. However, claim C48 regarding stereoscopic depth perception is more speculative, appropriately qualified with 'assuming that this form of visual processing is available to and employed by the mouse' and supported by citations to relevant studies.

results.result: Direction-selective retinal ganglion cells show global alignment of their preferred orientations with cardinal directions of optic flow during idealized motion in mice.
results.evaluation: Claim C59 is directly cited from Sabbah et al., 2017, an established study on retinal organization. This provides mechanistic support for how the retina may be organized to process optic flow patterns, though it is supporting context rather than a primary finding of the current study.

results.result: Torsional eye rotations in freely moving mice are dynamic and correlated with both head pitch and head roll, extending previous findings in rats. Models incorporating both pitch and roll predict torsional rotations better than pitch-alone models (reducing error from ~7° to lower values).
results.evaluation: Claim C60 appropriately cites rat literature (Wallace et al., 2013). Claims C61-C62 provide new data on mouse torsional dynamics with correlation coefficients for both pitch and roll. Claim C63 quantifies model improvement when including both axes. The evidence is supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2 with adequate sample sizes (N=4406 detect and N=13624 track frames from N=3 mice).

results.result: The coordinate system registration between environmental digitization and mouse/cricket tracking achieved sub-millimeter accuracy (mean differences <1 mm in all three dimensions).
results.evaluation: Claim C69 provides specific quantitative accuracy metrics (x: 0.18±3.1mm, y: 0.07±1.6mm, z: 0.66±1.8mm) based on N=54 fiducial points from three datasets. This technical validation is important for establishing the reliability of the visual field reconstruction method, though it is a methodological detail rather than a primary scientific finding.

results.result: Crickets provided suitable prey targets that could evade capture for extended periods (64.4±39.3s), and TiO2 corneal marks used for torsion tracking did not significantly affect hunting performance.
results.evaluation: Claim C84 provides descriptive statistics with citation to previous work (Hoy et al., 2016). Claim C85 is supported by Figure 7C showing no significant difference in capture times with TiO2 marks. These are important methodological validations ensuring the experimental manipulations did not confound the behavioral measurements.

results.result: Sensitivity analysis of the eye model showed that variations of 10-100 μm in optical parameters produced maximum deviations of 0.4-2.76 degrees, which would not influence the study's conclusions.
results.evaluation: Claim C86 provides quantitative sensitivity analysis with specific parameter variations and resulting angular deviations, supported by Figure 7E. This validation is important for establishing the robustness of the eye model used to project retinal features onto the cornea, though it is a technical validation rather than a primary finding.

results.result: Mice possess a large panoramic visual field (~200° monocular fields) that is stabilized by VOR-driven eye rotations. The retina contains diverse RGC types with spatially segregated distributions, and retinal subregions are thought to be tuned for specific behavioral tasks.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C7-C11 are well-established facts from the literature, appropriately cited from multiple sources (Dräger, 1978; Hughes, 1979; Meyer et al., 2020; Baden et al., 2016; Bleckert et al., 2014; etc.). These provide essential background context for the study but are not novel findings. The claims accurately represent the cited literature.

results.result: Experiments used male C57Bl/6J mice aged 2-8 months (21-29g) and crickets with body sizes of 1-2 cm.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68 provide basic experimental details stated in Materials and Methods. These are straightforward methodological descriptions that are adequately documented but represent standard reporting rather than findings requiring evaluation.
